The lander was named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station, in Ares Vallis.

checkpoints.title: CHECKPOINT 1 // THE ARRIVAL
checkpoints.log: SYSTEM LOG 01: I am Sojourner, the first rover to ever rove another planet! My Pathfinder lander cushioned our arrival with giant airbags—we bounced 15 times, up to 50 feet high, and rolled 1 kilometer to rest at the Carl Sagan Memorial Station in Ares Vallis.

checkpoints.title: CHECKPOINT 2 // THE PIONEER
checkpoints.log: SYSTEM LOG 02: Standing just 1 foot tall and weighing 23 pounds, I deployed down a 20-degree ramp into this ancient flood plain. Navigating these massive boulders takes serious verticality, so my Airbag Bounce system is keeping me moving forward!

checkpoints.title: CHECKPOINT 3 // THE GREAT DISCOVERY
checkpoints.log: SYSTEM LOG 03: My sensors are rewriting planetary science! I've spotted rounded pebbles that suggest water once flowed across a warmer Mars. Plus, our Pathfinder mission discovered the airborne dust is magnetic and spotted early-morning water ice clouds!

codex.file: Archive File: Mars Pathfinder & Sojourner (The Pioneers)

sections.heading: Mission Profile
sections.body: Launched on December 4, 1996, Mars Pathfinder and its rover, Sojourner, landed on July 4, 1997, in Ares Vallis—a rocky, ancient flood plain in Mars' northern hemisphere. The lander was named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station.

sections.heading: The Landing & Hardware
sections.body: Pathfinder pioneered an innovative airbag landing system that bounced about 15 times—reaching up to 50 feet high—and rolled roughly 1 kilometer from its initial impact point before coming to a stop. Sojourner, standing just 1 foot tall and weighing 23 pounds, deployed down a 20-degree ramp to explore the surface.

sections.heading: Major Discoveries
sections.body: The mission's observations of rounded pebbles suggested that flowing liquid water existed during a warmer period in Mars' past. The mission also discovered that airborne Martian dust has magnetic properties and observed early-morning clouds composed of water ice.

sections.heading: Mission Legacy
sections.body: Before its final transmission on September 27, 1997, the Pathfinder mission returned 2.3 billion bits of information, proving that low-cost mobile exploration on the Red Planet was possible.

notes: Arcade ability inspired by Pathfinder’s landing airbags; Sojourner did not jump.
The 2.3 billion bits and the roughly 1 kilometer of bounce-and-roll travel belong to the whole Pathfinder mission (lander and rover); Sojourner itself drove about 100 meters.
Magnetic-dust power drain, hopping and the airbag bounce are arcade abstractions, not literal rover capabilities.
